title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Myoclonic epilepsy of infancy (MEI), also known as benign myoclonic epilepsy in infancy, is a rare, self-limited epileptic syndrome characterized by brief myoclonic seizures in previously healthy and developmentally normal children. The syndrome is classified under idiopathic generalized epilepsies with age-related onset. Symptoms typically emerge within the first 3 years of life, with seizures involving rapid, synchronized jerks primarily affecting the head and upper extremities. Consciousness is usually preserved, though mild alterations can occur during seizure clusters. A third of cases report febrile seizures and a family history of epilepsy is common in about 30% of patients.

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Diagnosis often involves polygraphic electroencephalography, which may reveal characteristic patterns during seizures and neuroimaging. Sodium valproate is the preferred treatment, achieving seizure control in most cases. The prognosis for MEI is generally favorable, allowing for the eventual tapering of medications in many patients. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in recognizing MEI and differentiating it from similar seizure disorders, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional management approach to improve patient outcomes.

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Introduction
content: Myoclonic epilepsy of infancy (MEI) is a rare self-limited epileptic syndrome characterized by brief myoclonic seizures in previously healthy and developmentally normal children with onset in the first 3 years of life. MEI is also known as benign myoclonic epilepsy in infants (BMEI), a term first used by Dravet and Bureau in a 1981 study. [1] Before this study, several similar cases had been reported but with varying terminology, including "myoclonic epilepsy of childhood," which was used by Jeavons. [2]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Introduction
content: MEI does not have a benign course or prognosis in some children, so the word benign was removed from the name. The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) has included MEI among other neonatal and infantile epileptic syndromes under the classification of idiopathic generalized epilepsies with age-related onset. [3] [4] [5] [6] However, MEI can present as a generalized epilepsy in a child with a developmental encephalopathy or normal intellect. [7]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Etiology
content: MEI may be an early form of a genetic type of idiopathic generalized epilepsy. A genetic cause has been suggested for MEI, which is supported by a few specific genetic abnormalities that have been identified, eg, SLC2A1 and HCN4 mutations. [8] [9]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Etiology
content: Additionally, two-thirds of MEI occur spontaneously, while one-third are induced by trigger factors, including sudden noise, touch, or light, termed reflex variant MEI. Among the reflex variant MEI, 20% may be triggered by photic stimulation, and approximately 80% induced by the sudden acoustic or tactile stimulus. [10] [11]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Epidemiology
content: MEI is an uncommon condition and accounts for 1% to 2% of childhood epilepsy, which may be a slight underestimate of the actual situation. [12] Males are twice as likely to be affected as females. MEI occurs primarily in children aged 6 months to 2 years. However, MEI can occur in children as young as 4 months and as old as 5 years. [13]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- History and Physical
content: MEI occurs in previously healthy and developmentally normal children. Usually, there will be no significant past medical history except for a history of febrile seizures in one-third of cases. A positive family history of seizures in first and second-degree relatives is noted in 30% of cases. [13]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- History and Physical
content: Myoclonic seizures are the only type of seizures occurring in MEI. MEI is characterized by myoclonic jerks that occur as either a brief solitary episode (1 to 2 secs) or a cluster of 2 to 8  involving predominantly the head and upper extremities. Myoclonic jerks are rapid, isolated, but simultaneous synchronous jerks of various muscle groups. Myoclonic seizures are often spontaneous, frequently occurring in wakefulness, less often during drowsiness or slow-wave sleep. The following features are noted in MEI: Myoclonic jerks involving upper extremities Head nodding, upward rolling of eyes, blinking Falls if standing with lower extremities involved Yelling or cough-like vocalization due to sudden diaphragmatic contraction (may sometimes accompany the myoclonic jerks) Consciousness is usually intact (mild alteration of consciousness can accompany a cluster of myoclonic seizures) [14] [15] The following variants of MEI have been reported:

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- History and Physical
content: Reflex myoclonic epilepsy of infancy (RMEI) : This is a peculiar subtype (10% of MEI) precipitated exclusively by sudden, unexpected tactile or auditory stimuli. RMEI is characterized by earlier onset, brief duration, a better prognosis with rapid remission, and better cognitive outcome. [16] [17] Photosensitive myoclonic epilepsy in infancy : This RMEI subtype is characterized by photic-induced myoclonic seizures, which are usually difficult to manage. Nocturnal MEI : The nocturnal variant of MEI in infancy has been reported in the literature, characterized by excessive myoclonic jerks only during sleep. [18] Familial infantile myoclonic epilepsy : Familial MEI with autosomal recessive inheritance (chromosome 16p13) has infantile-onset prolonged myoclonic status followed by generalized tonic-clonic seizure persisting into adulthood in all patients. [19]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Evaluation
content: Polygraphic electroencephalography (EEG) is a key component in the evaluation of MEI. The following EEG findings are observed in MEI: Normal EEG background activity Interictal EEG typically normal Ictal EEG reveals brief bursts of generalized spike-and-wave, polyspike, or polyspike-and-wave pattern with a frequency of 3 Hz Discharges corresponding to the myoclonus on electromyography (EMG) Activation of the EEG by sleep deprivation (20% of reflex MEI have photosensitivity, and photic stimulation can activate discharges) [16] [20]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Evaluation
content: Neuroimaging, eg, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has normal findings in patients with MEI, unlike Dravet syndrome or Lennox Gastaut syndrome. Genetic testing may be considered to rule out specific mutations.

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Treatment / Management
content: MEI has an excellent response to antiseizure medications. Sodium valproate (ie, valproic acid) is the drug of choice, and 80% of patients started on valproate become seizure-free. Clonazepam and levetiracetam are alternative drugs for MEI. [21] After 3 to 5 years from onset, antiseizure drug therapy can be gradually weaned over months. RMEI with acoustic and somatosensory triggered myoclonus may not need treatment or be weaned after 1 year. RMEI with photosensitivity is more challenging to control, and levetiracetam is the most potent antimyoclonic antiseizure medication, suppressing photosensitivity. [22]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Treatment / Management
content: Other forms of myoclonic epilepsy discussed under differential diagnosis are challenging to treat. The primary treatment modalities for West syndrome are ACTH/corticosteroids or vigabatrin. Clobazam, sodium valproate, and zonisamide may be second-line drugs. First-line medications for Dravet syndrome are a combination of antiseizure drugs (eg, clobazam and valproic acid); alternative treatment includes stiripentol, topiramate, fenfluramine, ketogenic diet, or vagus nerve stimulation. [23]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Treatment / Management
content: Antiseizure drugs, eg, felbamate, lamotrigine, topiramate, and rufinamide, have been tried for seizures associated with Lennox Gastaut syndrome. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a cannabidiol oral solution to treat seizures associated with Lennox Gastaut syndrome or Dravet syndrome in patients aged 2 years and older. [24]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Hypnagogic jerks : Benign myoclonic jerks that usually occur when falling asleep characterize this condition. They are also called Hypnic jerks or sleep starts, and they resemble the jerks of myoclonic seizures. Hypnagogic jerks do not occur in waking states; the EEG is normal. [25]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Benign nonepileptic myoclonus of infancy : Also called benign spasm of infancy, patients with this condition have nonepileptic spasms occurring in the first year of life, which spontaneously resolve by 2 years of age. Benign nonepileptic myoclonus of infancy is characterized by spasms lasting 1 to 2 seconds, with normal ictal and interictal EEG recordings. Ictal video EEG helps in ruling out the epileptic myoclonus of infancy and thereby helps to avoid unnecessary or over-treatment. [26]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Benign neonatal sleep myoclonus : This is a spontaneously resolving condition featured by myoclonic lightning-like jerks occurring only during nonrapid eye movement sleep, with normal EEG findings. However, MEI is typically noted to have onset after 6 months of age and generally does not happen during sleep, which is an important distinctive feature. [27] [28]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Differential Diagnosis -- Epileptic Encephalopathies
content: Dravet syndrome : Also called  severe myoclonic epilepsy in infancy (SMEI), this is a pharmaco-refractory epilepsy in previously healthy children with the onset in the first year of life. SMEI is usually a channelopathy often caused by SCN1A mutation in 75% of patients. The seizures are usually prolonged, refractory, febrile or nonfebrile, and generalized or unilateral clonic. Temperature sensitivity and onset with febrile seizures can be seen, with normal EEG initially. As seizures progress, developmental delay with cognitive impairment and behavior disorders are possible in the long run. Neuroimaging is usually normal, and interictal EEG may be abnormal with generalized or focal slowing. [29] [30]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Differential Diagnosis -- Epileptic Encephalopathies
content: West syndrome (infantile spasms) : West syndrome is characterized by the triad of infantile spasms, an abnormal EEG with Hypsarrhythmia, and developmental arrest. [31]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Differential Diagnosis -- Epileptic Encephalopathies
content: Lennox Gastaut syndrome : Characteristic features of this syndrome are a triad of multiple seizures (ie, tonic seizures in sleep, myoclonic, and atypical absence seizures), an abnormal EEG with a slow spike-and-wave pattern, and developmental arrest. Lennox Gastaut syndrome presents later in childhood than infantile spasms and can be preceded by West's syndrome in 20% of cases. [32]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Differential Diagnosis -- Epileptic Encephalopathies
content: Progressive myoclonic epilepsies (PME) : PME comprises a group of rare types of epilepsies that are progressive. PME includes Lafora body disease, Unverricht-Lundborg disease, mitochondrial encephalopathy with ragged-red fibers, type 3 neuronopathic Gaucher Disease, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, and sialidosis. PME typically presents in late childhood or adolescence. The characteristic features of PME are multiple seizures (myoclonic or tonic-clonic), progressive neurologic deterioration including ataxia, or dementia. [33]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Prognosis
content: MEI usually remits within 6 months to 5 years from onset. RMEI induced by auditory or tactile stimuli has a better prognosis and an excellent antiseizure drug response. However, the photosensitive reflex variant is difficult to manage, and EEG photosensitivity persists several years after clinical remission. Approximately one-fifth of patients with MEI develop afebrile generalized tonic-clonic seizures later in the clinical course when the antiseizure drug is withdrawn. Two-thirds of patients with MEI have normal psychomotor development, and approximately one-third develop mild cognitive, behavioral, or motor deficits. Early-onset seizures and poor seizure control are risk factors for a poor neuropsychological outcome. [34]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Complications
content: Seizures in MEI typically resolve; However, some patients have a recurrence of seizures in adolescence. Febrile seizures occur in a higher proportion. Afebrile generalized tonic-clonic seizures occur in 20% of MEI. Development of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and focal epilepsies have been reported rarely.

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Complications
content: Neuropsychological deficits, including fine motor skill deficits, attention deficits, cognitive problems, language impairment, and learning disorders, are observed in long-term follow-ups of patients with MEI. Early-onset recurrent seizures can increase the risk of cognitive deficits. [35]

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Complications
content: Treatment-related adverse effects include behavior and mood disorders with levetiracetam, thrombocytopenia, and hepatotoxicity with sodium valproate. Due to its increased hepatotoxicity, sodium valproate is avoided in children younger than 2 years. Monitoring drug levels and checking hematological parameters and liver enzymes are essential to prevent complications.

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Consultations
content: A neuropsychological evaluation is important for children with long-standing epilepsy, as cognitive and learning problems will be coexistent. Consultations with genetic specialists and counselors are important in familial and also progressive myoclonic epilepsies.

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Parents or caretakers of the patient need to be counseled about the self-limiting nature of the condition. If antiseizure drugs are started for MEI, the risk-benefits of antiseizure medications should be discussed. Despite MEI being self-limiting and benign, MEI patients need careful follow-up to look for neuropsychological deficits, educational difficulties, and resurgence of seizures in the long run. Counseling about potential adverse effects and complications is essential, emphasizing specific safety profiles of the antiseizure drugs.

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: An integrated, interprofessional approach is essential for optimal patient-centered care for children with MEI. Primary care clinicians, including pediatricians and nurse practitioners, play a critical role in the early identification of MEI, ruling out other epilepsy syndromes and minimizing unnecessary diagnostic evaluation. Long-term follow-up with neurologists and primary care clinicians is vital, as MEI patients face risks of seizure recurrence in adulthood and neuropsychiatric deficits. Nurses and nurse practitioners support families by educating them on seizure safety, medication adherence, and the importance of regular follow-ups. They also serve as liaisons between families and clinicians, ensuring patient concerns are addressed and care plans are reinforced.

title: Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Pharmacists enhance care by educating families on proper medication use, monitoring for adverse effects, managing drug-drug interactions, and supporting clinicians during antiseizure medication weaning. Social workers help identify and address social barriers to care, ensuring families can access necessary resources. Psychologists play a key role in evaluating and addressing cognitive or learning disabilities, often recommending individualized education plans in collaboration with schools. Effective communication and care coordination among primary care clinicians, neurologists, nurses, pharmacists, social workers, psychologists, and the patient’s family are essential to improving outcomes, enhancing patient safety, and ensuring comprehensive, team-based care for children with MEI.
